name: 名古屋市市政資料館 喫茶室 (Nagoya City Archives Kissashitsu)

claims.text: No information about gluten cross-contamination precautions is available from any source. The kitchen prepares wheat-bread sandwiches and toast as its core menu items, making a gluten-safe environment unlikely.

No soy sauce is listed as an ingredient in menu items. The menu is limited to sandwiches, toast, and beverages, so soy sauce exposure risk is minimal, but no explicit allergen information is provided.
Sandwiches contain egg and ham. No vegan-separated prep area or dedicated utensils are mentioned. Beverages appear plant-based but are not explicitly labeled vegan.

No allergen menu, allergy protocol, or staff allergy-handling practice has been documented in any available source. Phone ahead (052-953-0051) to inquire directly before visiting with a serious allergy.
Menu is very short and simple — sandwiches, toast, and drinks — so ingredient questions are straightforward to ask. Staff are consistently described as friendly and approachable.
Entirely non-smoking environment inside a civic building.

name: なごや えんきょ (Nagoya Enkyo)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free kitchen or cross-contamination controls are described. Omakase production in a compact kitchen handling soy sauce, miso, and breaded or battered items creates real shared-surface risk.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (containing wheat) is almost certainly used throughout. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere on the official site or third-party listings.
All courses include fish-based dashi (red dashi miso soup confirmed), sashimi, and meat. Animal products are integral to every course component; no plant-only preparation line exists.
The menu page asks guests to notify the restaurant of allergies in advance, but no specific allergy protocol, substitution policy, or staff training is described.

Advance notice is explicitly requested for allergies, and the intimate counter format means the single chef oversees all preparation — reducing the risk of miscommunication between kitchen staff compared to large restaurants.
No information on cross-contamination controls available; standard machi-chuka kitchen implies shared woks and utensils used across all dishes.

Wheat-containing soy sauce is a foundational ingredient in Chinese restaurant cooking and almost certainly used across sauces, marinades, and stir-fry bases here; no tamari or GF soy sauce alternative mentioned.
Shared wok cooking with meat, pork mince (Taiwan dishes), and animal-based stocks makes vegan cross-contact unavoidable.

name: 名古屋名物 みそかつ 矢場とん 名古屋城 金シャチ横丁店 (Nagoya Meibutsu Misokatsu Yabaton Nagoya Cas)

claims.text: Every item on the menu is deep-fried in a shared fryer environment. There is no documentation of a dedicated gluten-free fryer, a gluten-free menu section, or any separation protocol for wheat-sensitive guests.

The miso sauce is the centrepiece of the dish. The retail version of the sauce lists soy (大豆), pork, and rice as declared allergens without separately listing wheat; however, Nagoya red-miso (豆味噌/八丁味噌) is traditionally made from soybeans only and does not inherently contain wheat — but the restaurant's full preparation environment cannot be verified as wheat-free.
The kitchen is entirely pork-focused; pork fat, pork-based miso sauce, and deep-frying in shared oil used for pork cutlets make any vegan cross-contact unavoidable.

No allergen-accommodation procedures, allergy menus, or staff allergy-handling protocols are published on the Tabelog listing, official website, or Kinshachi Yokocho shop page. A Yahoo Chiebukuro report notes that a customer with a dairy allergy was told by Yabaton that their fried items contain milk components, suggesting the kitchen does respond to direct inquiries but has no documented systematic allergy protocol.
Cards and electronic payments accepted (VISA, MC, JCB, AMEX, Diners, Suica, iD, QUICPay, etc.) — easy for foreign visitors without cash.

name: 名古屋とうふ 河口 金シャチ横丁店 (Nagoya Tofu Kawaguchi Kinshachi Yokocho)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free kitchen or certification. The stall operates within a busy shared market arcade; cross-contamination from neighboring stalls (soba, tempura) cannot be ruled out.

The dengaku miso is Hatcho-style (豆味噌 / 八丁味噌), brewed from soybeans and salt only — no wheat. This is a genuine GF advantage over standard miso or soy sauce-seasoned dishes. However, no public allergen sheet confirms total absence of wheat-based soy sauce from all preparations.
No animal-derived dashi or bonito detected in the core tofu or dengaku preparations. Soft serve dairy status is unconfirmed — verify at counter.
No public information about staff allergy training or allergy protocols. Phone: 052-231-8810 for advance inquiry.

Hatcho miso (豆味噌) used in dengaku contains only soybeans and salt — no wheat, unlike most soy sauces and many other miso types. Tofu itself is made from soybeans, nigari, and water with zero additives.

name: 名古屋城きしめん亭 (Nagoyajo Kishimen-tei)

claims.text: Kishimen noodles are made from wheat flour — gluten is the primary ingredient. No GF alternative exists. The kitchen also prepares tempura and fried items in the same space.
The dashi broth is seasoned with standard soy sauce, which contains wheat. No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce option is mentioned anywhere.
Bonito flakes (katsuobushi) are a direct topping on kishimen and are also used in the broth base. There is no plant-based broth option. All menu items contain animal-derived ingredients.

This is a traditional Japanese fugu counter. Wheat flour is used in fried fugu preparation (kara-age) and wheat-based soy sauce is standard in ponzu and seasoning throughout the menu. Cross-contamination risk in a tiny 8-seat counter kitchen with no separation of cooking surfaces must be assumed.
No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned in any review or listing. Traditional wheat-containing shoyu is the default for ponzu dipping and cooking.
Every component of the menu involves fugu or fish-derived stock. There is no vegan menu path and no plant-based preparation area.

No information on allergy communication or accommodation has been published. Given this is a tiny counter run by two people with no English-language presence, allergy discussions would need to happen in Japanese at the time of reservation.

The restaurant is non-smoking throughout (全席禁煙), and fugu itself — as a white fish served as sashimi or in broth — is naturally free of gluten when prepared without soy sauce or flour coating. Guests with specific needs should raise this at booking.

name: 日本料理 丈 (Nihon Ryori Jo)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free preparation area or cross-contamination protocols are disclosed. A kaiseki kitchen uses wheat-based shoyu and mirin routinely across multiple dishes; shared prep surfaces and equipment are the norm in this format.

Standard Japanese kaiseki relies on shoyu (soy sauce brewed with wheat) as a foundational seasoning in sauces, marinades, and finishing. No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere in available sources.

Dashi (stock) in kaiseki is typically made with katsuobushi (bonito flakes) or niboshi (dried sardines) and is used throughout the menu — in soups, sauces, and seasonings. No plant-based dashi option is advertised.

The official site states that allergy and dietary concerns must be communicated at the time of reservation. No adjustments are guaranteed after arrival. Guests with serious allergies should call 052-908-8930 (10:00–18:30) before booking.

The counter omakase format ('御誂え料理') allows the kitchen to pace and adjust individual courses in real time, which in principle creates more opportunity for dietary discussion than a fixed set menu — though this is subject to advance notice at booking.
